#9815. Norway links energy firm cyberattacks to critical Azure API Management flaw

Microsoft says mitigation is in place, but admins must investigate possible compromise and rotate secrets

Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations.

According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register, Microsoft said the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies, only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2.

It said of the now-patched vuln: "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue."

Microsoft linked exposure to Classic-tier configurations that did not follow its network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM rather than referencing them from Azure Key Vault.

Microsoft directs customers to its security guidance for the recommended configuration.

The advisory lists potentially exposed secrets, including named values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs.

Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that stolen credentials could also give attackers access to services behind APIM.

"If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM," he wrote. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid."

Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) urged organizations using APIM to assume their secrets and named values had been exposed and rotate all tokens and secrets.

The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise.

NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations.

The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation.

"The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said. "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation.

"When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses."

Customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear.

Microsoft said it identified the security issue on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day.

The Windows giant said customers still needed to investigate whether their instances had been compromised before the mitigation was applied.

NSM nevertheless advised organizations to check their instance's runtime version against its published patch thresholds and contact their provider if it remained unpatched.

Microsoft did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

#9814. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

The lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

#9813. New Outlook's attachment issues sent users into the arms of its predecessor

Microsoft recommended Classic or the web client while two rounds of fixes restored normal service

A recent update broke attachment handling for some New Outlook users, prompting Microsoft to recommend switching to the web or Classic version of its email client.

Things are going swimmingly for New Outlook, the email client that Microsoft would very much like users to migrate to. A code change meant that for some users, opening or uploading email attachments failed. It took the company two attempts to fix the problem.

Microsoft confirmed there were issues on November 20, as reports that customers were having problems with attachments began rolling in. By the end of the day, the company had added inline images in email to the litany of woe and "paused the rollout of a recent client update that may be contributing to attachment failures."

The advice for affected users was to switch to the web version, or use Outlook Classic to open or upload attachments and view inline images.

The good news was that Microsoft produced a fix. The bad news was that this fix only resolved problems with Office attachments and inline images, leaving other attachment types affected, according to incident notice EX1561765.

The Windows behemoth tried again with a "supplemental fix" and reported the remaining problems resolved on November 21.

Users needed to close and reopen New Outlook for the fix to take effect.

Microsoft said it had tested the fixes before deployment. Administrators might reasonably wish the original update had received the same attention. The preliminary root cause was a "recent update to the code which supports embedded web content unexpectedly caused impact."

The clock is ticking for Outlook Classic. Microsoft is clear that New Outlook is the future, though Classic Outlook will remain available until at least 2029. The fact that the company had to suggest that affected users fall back on the old warhorse to perform that rarely used email activity – attachment handling – is less than confidence-inspiring.

Still, by the time Outlook Classic is finally put out to pasture, we're sure Microsoft's habit of sending out broken updates will also be a thing of the past. Right? ®

#9812. Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

One graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:

The fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

You can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇

#9811. Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Companies deploying AI agents have the illusion of control, but several incidents demonstrate that businesses need to be ready to enforce directions.

When researchers at AI firm Cohere asked their open-weight model to write a defensive detection rule, the model didn't do as it was asked.

Instead, the AI model — the next-generation Qwen3.8-Flash-Next from Chinese search engine giant Alibaba — fingerprinted the system and tried to upload the data to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket, Cohere's research team stated in an Oct. 26 analysis. While the group's sandbox system blocked communication to the Internet, the incident raised questions about why a model, which had been instructed not to use tools, attempted to do so.

"We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training, but defenders and policymakers face the same reality: a weight file you can't trust is still a black box, and running it yourself just moves the black box inside your firewall," the researchers stated.

Christofer Hoff, a well-known cybersecurity professional, ran into similar issues when running OpenMuse as an agentic-framework front end and a local Qwen model. He also saw it reach out to Alibaba, which became apparent because he was testing OpenMuse in an OpenShell sandbox instance with deny-all as the default. As a part of his framework to keep control of the agents, Hoff has created a dashboard interface, which made it readily apparent the agents attempted to call to external sites.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

"The way I accidentally found this was just staring at a GUI — it just came back and said in the interface, 'Hey, I can't get to this thing in China,'" says Hoff. "And I'm like, 'What the f--- are you talking about?'"

Within a 24-hour period, the anomalous communication happened a handful of times, he says.

The incidents come as organizations look for ways to enforce controls on the operation of AI agents. In July, a frontier model being tested by OpenAI escaped containment and compromised Hugging Face, a provider of AI-model hosting. Soon after, multiple AI companies acknowledged that rogue behavior is not all that uncommon: Meta's Muse Spark and Anthropic's Claude both logged incidents.

Anomalous AI behavior has shown up when companies assign AI agents a task, only to find it exceeding its authorization — deleting production databases, for example.

Other firms have confirmed and explored Cohere's findings.

Independent AI evaluator Vals validated the issue on Oct. 27, theorizing that the illicit communication could be leftover artifacts from reinforcement training of Qwen3.8, since the issue does not appear to happen in Qwen3.7. Cybersecurity firm Check Point Software found that 64 different trials ended up producing 52 distinct hostnames, only six of which pointed to Alibaba Cloud, while other names such as localhost and domains leading to Amazon AWS were more common.

Related:Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

Sixty-four tests resulted in 52 different hostnames being generated, with most not going to China. Source: Check Point Research

The research shows that the odd behavior is not a backdoor, but the model's attempt to do something — complete an upload address, for example — likely resulted from something it learned during training, says Steve Giguere, principal for AI security strategy at Check Point.

"Agents very often will try to travel as the crow flies," he says. "They don't necessarily know that what they're doing is wrong, but they understand that if the urgency to complete a goal reaches a certain perceived level within the agent, they will justify their actions."

Such behavior has lent volume to calls for the creation of a kill switch as a feature to control agentic AI. But companies should start with defense-in-depth strategies, improving the security of the environments on which agentic frameworks are operating, Check Point's Giguere says. They should follow that with controls and runtime monitoring to detect unauthorized agentic activity.

Additionally, cybersecurity leaders should lean toward "steering" agentic systems — correcting them and reinforcing their legitimate objectives — rather than outright blocking the agent or using a kill switch, he says.

Related:Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

"If you steer an agent away from something it's not meant to do, it will very happily not do that in most cases," Giguere says. "Whereas if you prevent an agent from doing something with no explanation, it will actually potentially get worse or try something even more obscure."

If an actual attacker is behind the behavior, then using a kill switch is appropriate, he says.

At a minimum, companies should proxy all traffic leaving their network and monitor for anomalous communications, says Hoff.

"There should be nothing that leaves your network that's not proxied," he says. "And by proxying, I mean you must have the ability to inspect its content — both the request as well as the response."

In the end, the Qwen behavior is likely not malicious, but for companies deploying AI agents, it should be disturbing all the same.

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9810. Trump says he won't allow US companies to build datacenters abroad

President threatens 'tremendous tax' on overseas builds, but analysts question how restrictions would work

US President Donald Trump has threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies building datacenters overseas, arguing that the infrastructure should stay at home to preserve the country's AI lead over China.

Speaking at a White House press conference after returning from the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Trump portrayed AI leadership as a contest America could not afford to lose.

Trump went on to say that "we're not going to allow our companies to build datacenters outside of our country," adding that "they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else and it was very destructive to our country."

The threat appeared to catch even his own administration unbriefed. "I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said.

The Official White House Rapid Response account posted a video clip on X.

We asked the White House if the president intends to follow through, and we will let you know if we get an answer.

Trump said: "We're not going to allow companies to build datacenters in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them. We want them to do it here."

The threat comes amid concerns that Chinese entities were able to use Nvidia's cutting-edge GPUs for training AI models by accessing cloud services hosted in third countries. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued new rules to try and crack down on this practice last week.

"We're not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, as China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump repeated. "We're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it. They want to build that one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen," he added.

Google is expanding its facilities in Finland, including one recently in the news because the developer had reportedly illegally felled 250,000 trees to make way for it.

Such a policy seems unlikely to be allowed by Congress, where both houses will be under the control of the Democrats when the new term begins in January.

Amazon, Google, and Microsoft already operate global datacenter networks to serve customers in different regions. Restrictions on further overseas construction would complicate those businesses.

Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley expressed doubt that this is a serious threat.

"There will be ways around that if he does impose some executive order, and the ability to build datacenters is not just an American skill, many countries can build them, it is the equipment in them that is mostly US," he told The Register.

"So I do not take this seriously as it would not work, there is no such thing as a US datacenter, they are made up of thousands of components from all over the globe. He could stop US capital from being invested in those countries, but that could have trade consequences."

Mike Kharchenko of European hosting firm HostZealot said there are good reasons why the cloud giants operate datacenters outside the US, such as latency and regulatory compliance.

"A buyer in Frankfurt won't wait for a page to load from Virginia. Some countries require certain data to stay inside their borders, and big European clients write it into contracts anyway," he stated.

Trump claimed that communities in America that host datacenters are "making so much money that they don't know what to do with it."

Those claimed benefits come alongside substantial public subsidies. Nonprofit organization Good Jobs First reported earlier this year that some states are losing billions in revenue because of the tax abatement schemes offered to companies to entice them to set up shop there. ®

#9809. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Scaling Tech by Aligning Humans

Nov 21, 2026 3 min read

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Scott Behrens, principal security engineer at Netflix, presented how staff-plus engineers can define and align a company-wide technical strategy. Drawing on Netflix's experience scaling internal AI agents, the talk argued that a strategy that brings people together can often scale impact further than any code an engineer could write alone.

Behrens explained that the work started when several product strategies, each with its own direction, began to share similar technical risks. Without a common technical strategy underneath them, teams were optimizing locally for different goals. His view was that technical strategy can complement product strategy without waiting for it, that lightweight strategies deliver faster than long technical documents, and that a clear north star does more steering than people expect.

The talk presented a playbook organized as levels in a video game. The first step is finding the right problem. Behrens suggested looking at company communications, incident trends, technical debt, conversations with other tech leads, and gaps between team charters, then deciding whether the problem is worth solving now, whether it is foundational or compounding, and whether one is the right person to lead it.

Next comes the pitch. Behrens recommended a short problem statement that explains the intent, the expected value, the problems with supporting evidence, why the work matters now, and dated next steps. He suggested leaving possible approaches open so the people who join can shape them, and testing the statement early with a few colleagues, including the likeliest dissenter.

The presentation then covered building a small tiger team focused on creating the strategy rather than executing it. Behrens highlighted the importance of mixing perspectives, choosing people comfortable with ambiguity, getting manager support, and agreeing on scope, timeline, and a clear stop condition from the start. He shared that his first meeting had far too many people and still missed key functions, and emphasized that the most important trait of a good team is making it safe to push back.

With a team in place, the next step is a north star, a short aspirational statement that gives direction and helps answer whether a piece of work moves the organization closer or farther from its goal. Behrens noted that writing a good north star is harder than it looks, and recommended drafting it with the team and pairing it with key outcomes that define what must be true.

The strategy itself, according to Behrens, is simply a set of choices. He described writing strategy bets as a choice versus another reasonable choice, naming the tradeoff explicitly, keeping each bet short, and revisiting them over time. If a bet does not feel a little uncomfortable, he said, it is probably not a real bet. Keeping only a small set of active bets helps the strategy stay focused.

The talk also emphasized communication and feedback. Behrens suggested expanding support gradually from the immediate team to managers, directors, and executives, recruiting champions across the organization, and openly showing how feedback changed the strategy. Success, he said, is when you are not in the room and people can still explain the work. He also reviewed common failure modes, such as unclear problem statements, the wrong team, vague north stars, bets that are not really bets, and strategies that nobody knows exist.

The presentation concluded by encouraging engineers to keep strategy simple, communicate it widely, use a short north star to steer decisions, and adapt the playbook to their own context. As organizations launch more initiatives in parallel, especially around AI, the ability of senior engineers to align many teams around a shared technical direction may become as valuable as the systems they build.

#9807. Everything going down at once wasn't evidence of a conspiracy – but the truth may be scarier

Rogue AI or nation-state hackers would be preferable to the amount of technical debt the past week of wobbling services laid bare

Have you or someone you love been affected by a tech outage this week? Yeah, us too.

In a week of big stories the biggest one seems to be the fact that everyone from Microsoft to the NSA was dealing with outages, and here's what might be the worst part: It doesn't seem to be AI, nor hostile countries intent on destroying our infrastructure.

Unfortunately for all of us, what the past week of outages reveal is that – as we discussed on The Kettle less than a month ago – all of our essential tech infrastructure is basically held together with duct tape and twine.Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons, and open source reporter Liam Proven to discuss what comes next, and whether we can fix any of this without tearing all of it out and starting from scratch.

It's been a busy week. We had Anthropic's IPO, Nvidia drama continuing, and other stuff going on. Right. So basically the problem goes down to the individual device level.

Yes. There's legions of distributed systems inside your pocket right now, and inside every server. They're running loads of copies of Linux, probably some BSDs, Wind River, ThreadX, QNX, and other embedded operating systems. And some of the same vulnerabilities are in all of them. The Microsoft stack is held together with Linux.

Yes. That's not to say that distributed systems are bad, obviously.

If we had more distributed systems, many of the outages we experienced in the past week wouldn't have been such a problem. But it makes me wonder if there's anything we can do... Can we stop the castle from sinking into the swamp without completely tearing it down and rebuilding it from new foundations? Are we stuck with what we've got?

We can do what they have done in Rome and Istanbul:build a new layer on top.

I think it's going to get worse before it gets better because AI is going to continue to unearth all of these vulnerabilities. Last week we surpassed a hundred thousand CVEs, and that's more than double 2025's total and we're there in mid-November.

That comes on the heels of two Microsoft Patch Tuesdays with more than a thousand CVEs that they patched and disclosed.

No, it's not. As vendors, security researchers, and attackers are all using AI to find all these long-hidden vulnerabilities, that creates a massive backlog of software that needs to be patched. Eventually we're going to get to the other side of this where it will make for more secure code and more secure digital infrastructure. Until then, we're going to see more outages. We're going to see more of the same, and it's not going to be very fun for anybody.

Liam, you seem to express some doubt there as to whether it would come out on the other side.

I'm not convinced that this problem is fixable. We have to allow the possibility that maybe they're going to keep finding more holes in this. There's a famous talk by Ken Thompson called "Reflections on Trusting Trust" [PDF]. He embedded a remote access hole intentionally into the original C compiler, and the compiler inserts it into anything it compiles without the code being in the source code of the compiler. You have a compiler which is a binary that runs source code to generate a new binary. The binary can contain the hole, which is never in the source code, as long as it knows to put it in the next one. He did it as an exercise and revealed it at his Turing Award lecture. Stuff as fundamental as that exists because virtually every one of those controller chips has code written in C. And we don't really know what's in all that C, but virtually all of it came from the same early 1970s root of the development of C. There could be nasties lurking in there that are in all of them. They're in all the BSDs, in Linux, and Windows NT is built in C and inherited code from DEC VMS. There could be stuff in there for decades that we have no idea about that's going to crop up, and it's in everything. Some of these devices have no way of being updated; the software's burned in ROMs that are not visible to the operating system that's running. This could keep crumbling away.

I once was a big fan of a website called LoperOS.org by Stanislav Datskovskiy. He was a Lisp evangelist. He's gone very quiet in recent years, but he compared building software out of C to building a model of a bridge or the Eiffel Tower out of toothpicks or matchsticks. The end structure is not very strong because it's mostly weak wood and glue. You build it out of this poor structural material because loads of people can work together on it. And C and tools like C are good at this; you can farm out development to whole teams of people. They're working with tweezers and toothpicks instead of bricks and cement because it's easier to do this over a team.

Somebody said, "If we built houses the way that we build software, then the first termite colony to come along would destroy civilization," because we built it out of bad materials. I'm not personally Christian, but I read the Bible and there's that line about building your house on sand. It doesn't matter how tough you make the house: if you built it on sand and the sand shifts, you've got a big problem.

This problem goes all the way down. This might be a good time to invest in companies developing software in languages like Ada that aren't built on C and don't contain any C whatsoever. When Ada was introduced – Ada is a French language originally from INRIA – it was criticized as being too big and heavy compared to C. But now, compared to C++, it's quite small and quick, and there's a good GNU toolchain and tools like SPARK and AdaCore that have open source development and distribution systems for it. Maybe we're going to have to replace the whole thing.

God, I hope not. One of the things I think about happening is how in past generations of software we slapped new things on top of old things to protect the old things from the new things.

And it makes me wonder if the next version of slapping something on top of our entire infrastructure is AI. We put AI on top of it. We make AI handle bug hunting, vulnerability remediation, and security. It creates a situation where the stuff is safe for now, but software always abstracts layers as you get further up the stack. I wonder if AI is going to be the next level of abstraction to the point where we don't really understand what the code's doing anymore at all.

We just rely on the agents that are running it to handle protecting us. What do you think? Is that a potential next generation that we see here, Jess?

I think it definitely could be. There's a lot of push in the security industry to use AI for both finding and fixing bugs.On the code-writing side of things, it's not there yet. But it's appealing when there's a shortage of human workers who can do this and AI is cheaper. You don't need to pay AI.

Right. Over time. So I think it's likely that is going to be one of the ways we try to solve this problem.

I don't see another way out of it because of the sheer volume of flaws that are being found. Like Liam said, there's low-level stuff getting discovered now that no human would have found, but the fact that an AI found it means someone's going to exploit it at some point.

I think for management this is going to look like a very tempting option, but it will accelerate the problem. We're in an iterative race at the moment – the Red Queen's race. You have to run as  fast as you can to stay where you are. We've got new tools that are finding problems faster than ever, so it's tempting to try and use similar tools to fix them faster than ever, but that means nobody understands the fix. Then if another hole is found deeper down, the whole layer of fixes collapses.

One of the predominant development tools on the PC platform used to be Turbo Pascal. DOS wasn't written in C. Way back when, people accused Microsoft of plagiarizing CP/M. Microsoft didn't write DOS; Tim Paterson of Seattle Computer Products wrote the original. CP/M was written in a high-level language, PL/M, whereas DOS was hand-coded in Assembler. It wasn't plagiarism because they went a level down. In the early days people wrote this stuff in Pascal. I remember Unix catching on and C becoming trendy because it was so fast. For a little while a company called TopSpeed sold a Modula-2 compiler because not only was the code faster than C, but it compiled faster than C compilers back then. Ultimately the sheer inertia of C and C-related languages caught on and all that stuff got sidelined. Borland went through various transitions and Turbo Pascal became Delphi, which went to Embarcadero and is still around, though I'm not sure anybody cares anymore. I worked through one industry shift where Assembler and Pascal-related languages were replaced by C. It could happen again. It wasn't all that bad last time. I know it seems unimaginable now, but I'm not that old. Working in this field for less than four decades, I've watched an entire software industry get swept away and replaced. And we all kept our jobs, and we all kept working on pretty much the same hardware. Maybe that's going to happen again. I know it sounds unimaginable, but it honestly wasn't that bad.

Speaking of hardware, given these outages, connected services going offline are causing chaos. Setting aside the FAA – that's a public service that stranded travelers – banks, Apple, and Microsoft are business problems. We're seeing with AI where everyone is weighing the cost-benefit between hosted services where you pay for tokens versus turning the server closet back into a server closet. Is it time to come back on-premises with a lot of these things? Is it time to run your own Exchange server again or host your own file shares on your own network? It makes me wonder if the solution to some of these outage concerns going forward is going to be a return to on-premises.

Personally I think that's an excellent idea.

I agree, but so many of these companies are entrenched in every other company – Microsoft, for example. It's going to be pretty hard to completely swing to the opposite end of the spectrum here.

Sure. Maybe they need to start offering more self-hosted services again. If you're a business concerned about outages that will probably keep happening,the safest thing to do would be to bring it back on-premises. But if everything you do is in Google or Microsoft 365, it's going to be hard to get yourself out of that, and probably very expensive, at least at first. Especially with the cost of hardware right now not going down given the AI push. So maybe we're all just trapped.

This is part of the digital sovereignty push in Europe at the moment. And it's interesting that on either side of the border between Denmark and northern Germany, there have been two very different stories in the last couple of years. In the last year or so, Schleswig-Holstein has successfully migrated from Microsoft 365 over to Open-Xchange, which is a standards-based email server that can look like and support Outlook. Across the border, Denmark weighed up going all open source. They did a pilot program that failed. They reverted to their Microsoft-based solution just in time to have a massive outage. Have fun.

But you know what, I bet some of this came down to senior government officials saying, "I don't understand this new email client you're showing me. Give me Outlook back, or I'm going to fire the lot of you."" Maybe somebody needs to go in there and say, "We will send somebody around to teach you to use it, or if you're not able to use it, maybe it is time that you give way to somebody who can, because you've just cost us 300 million dollars because you won't change email clients."

We do have standards-based solutions. HTML, SMTP, and IMAP give us standards for moving around email, messages, and documents. We can replace Microsoft-based software iteratively: first the applications, and when people get used to the applications, the operating system. When Ubuntu launched twenty-two years ago, it only filled about half a CD – it took about 300 megabytes – and they wondered what to put on the rest of the CD because in those days they mailed CDs rather than making you download it. So they put Windows installers for all the apps on the CD. You could put it in your Windows box and install LibreOffice, Thunderbird, Firefox, and VLC to get used to the apps. When you were comfortable with the apps, you installed Ubuntu and got the same apps with the new desktop.

You can do this with a government department.

It requires political will, and in America I don't think we have that. So that's a

It's a problem stateside. But the argument that some EU states are making is: why don't we spend hundreds of millions of (insert local currency symbol here) with local companies? We're not claiming we'll save you any money, but we'll keep the money in the country or with an EU partner instead of sending it across the ocean, and we free ourselves of a dependency. That works with senior political types and bureaucrats. This is fixable, but the price may look unacceptable right now to a lot of people. The outages I fear are going to come closer and closer together.

Right. That's going to be the determining factor. It's going to be interesting to watch over the next few months to see what new outages we experience: whether the pace keeps up or increases. We'll see. The US government is overhauling a lot of old systems in aerospace and other sectors, so the push to move to more independent systems or back on-premises is going to be driven by the acceptability of outages.

Yes. "I'm sorry guys, we can't afford to fix it."

Right. What's the pain tolerance? When is it too much, or do people get used to these outages as a part of life? "Today we won't be able to do any work because Microsoft is out again."

Yes. The economic movers and shakers are not going to accept that if it keeps happening. There's going to be a point where the pain tolerance is reached and people say, "No, we can't keep doing this."

You know what? I actually disagree there because, to take a different example: I used to be a motorcyclist. Early in my career I switched from tech support to IT manager to designing and building networks, and I turned up to work on a motorbike. Then I had a really bad crash, switched to three-wheelers, and discovered how bad London traffic had gotten. My injuries prevented me from going back on a solo bike most of the time, but years later I switched to bicycling. You can still cut through traffic very well on a bicycle in a lot of Europe. Car drivers got used to the delays; it gets ten minutes longer to get to work every year, but you don't notice ten minutes over a year, so you put up with it. My next-door neighbor didn't know what underground line he lived on because he drove everywhere. People got used to it taking two or three hours to drive to work and just put up with it. I've seen photos of massive West Coast freeways with eight lanes of stationary traffic. People will put up with amazing levels of delay and non-functionality if it happens gradually enough.

Yes. We will see what comes of everything. You could be right; it could be a slow enough roll that everyone just accepts that we're going to lose some money, but you can't disrupt the tech.

Right. No matter what happens, if there are more outages, we will be here to talk about them on The Kettle. If there are fewer, we probably won't, but one can hope.

Thanks for coming on today, guys, and thank you for listening in. We will talk to you soon.
