#9738. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

#9736. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the company's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency and review.

Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web and TV.

Khuzam opened with a mock company email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The problem the team ran into next was summed up in one line.

The team's first attempt was having an agent migrate tests, and it took four tries. The team started with "migrate this file," then added instructions, then the APIs to use, then how to mock data.

The docs were also hard to find, since the agent's context window ran out before it found the right page. And they were inconsistent, because tests were not written the same way across the codebase.

Developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3. Moving from one test to a whole feature, from screen to data to route to test, meant teaching the agent how the team builds.

Khuzam described the fix as context engineering, "getting what engineers know into what agents see." The team wrote 45 architecture decision records, each "written for people and for agents."

Each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern and an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. It also links to related docs and code, and the records now ship inside almost every repository.

To keep those records and more than 300 other documents findable, the team borrowed from how search engines read a site. An AGENTS.md file, the project instructions file that coding agents read before anything else, plays the part of robots.txt.

The second half of the talk followed code after an agent writes it. Khuzam noted that the CI pipeline is still deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries.

What changed is how agents plug into each phase. A review agent pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns and looks at what depends on the change.

Its first version left 23 comments on a single PR, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same PR. Changes aren't yet auto-merged, and engineers own the code.

Khuzam reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and 32% more pull requests year over year. Developer NPS rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

Ahead of the session, Khuzam framed the stakes on LinkedIn: "Agents can write code, but what gives us the confidence to ship Tier 0 services to 300M+ members without everything falling apart?"

Work that crosses services raised a harder question. A product engineer building one feature touches the payment API, billing, the gateway and every client, so the team had to decide who owns the context and how it follows the work.

Khuzam listed approaches that did not hold up. Loading every repository did not fit, Git submodules were brittle, a Git MCP server "sees one file, not the system," and shared copies went stale.

The team needed context that was accurate, portable across agents, owned per domain and kept fresh. It settled on GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs.

Each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line.

Khuzam closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters. "None of this is new. It's good engineering, built for a new reader."

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the session and can view the session details here.

#9733. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:

<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:

Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:

The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:

The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

#9732. Swapping Jolt's sorted collections to a B+tree

Until recently, sorted-map and sorted-set in Jolt were a straight port of Clojure's PersistentTreeMap, which is backed by a persistent red-black tree. Using a red-black tree has worked well for Clojure, and it provides a solid foundation for backing these data structures. However, red-black trees have a downside, which is that every entry gets its own small node, meaning that every step of a lookup follows a pointer to a different place in memory.

So, naturally I got curious to see if a different data structure could be used for the same job which might have a lower overhead. Turns out that a red-black tree can indeed be swapped out for a B+tree here. I updated Jolt's sorted collections along with the java.util.TreeMap and TreeSet shims to use a persistent B+tree, which dropped peak memory by 40% while making most operations faster at every size, as we'll see later in the benchmarks.

Each red-black node in Jolt was a five-slot Scheme vector holding a color along with the key, the value, and its two children. And all that translates into 48 bytes of metadata per entry on top of the key and value themselves. A map with 4 million entries needs a tree around 22 levels deep, so, a lookup can end up visiting about 22 nodes scattered across the heap. And once the tree outgrows the CPU cache, each of these visits is likely to be a cache miss as well.

As you might've guessed, writes also have a similar problem. Since a persistent tree can't modify a node in place, an assoc has to copy every node on the path from the root to the change, which results in 22 small allocations followed by rebalancing at that size.

The key advantage of using a B+tree is that it keeps data in leaves of up to 16 entries and branches through inner nodes of up to 32 children with each node being a single Scheme vector. In this layout, a leaf is written as #(#t k0 v0 k1 v1 ...) with keys and values sitting side by side in one contiguous block. An inner node also stores the largest key below it right next to each child.

Now, the same tree of 4 million entries becomes just 5 levels deep instead of 22. On top of that, a lookup within each node has to only search through adjacent slots that are already in cache. Writes still have to copy the path from the root, but that's now a quarter of the work with each one being copied as a block.

Unsurprisingly, memory use improved significantly, since a full leaf holds 16 entries in 34 machine words, needing only 17 bytes per entry against the red-black tree's 48. Nodes are also allowed to drop to half before they merge, so 34 bytes per entry ends up being the worst case here. It would be ideal to keep the common case near full as much as possible, and a trick that can be used here is to start a fresh node when append goes past either end of the tree rather than splitting a full node into two half-empty ones. A common case for this would be building from ascending keys, which ends up packing every node using this approach. Similarly, deletes end up borrowing entries from a neighbour or merging with it to keep the tree balanced without needing rotations.

Of course, nothing in life is free, and B+trees do have a weakness of their own. While they're much faster for large collections, building small ones of tens to hundreds of entries one insert at a time ended up being around 15% slower than the red-black tree. The reason goes back to the respective structure of each data structure. Once a map has 17 entries, that requires a root with two leaves, and every insert needs to copy the whole path. So, at smaller sizes the B+tree has to move more bytes per insert than the red-black tree, which is the trade-off.

Luckily, there is a way around the problem by changing how collections get built. We can first collect the inputs for into, the sorted-map and sorted-set constructors, and multi-argument conj/assoc to check whether they're already in order, then skip the sort if they are. Additionally, we can drop duplicate keys by keeping the first key along with the last value, which allows us to bulk-load the leaves. The batches can now get merged with the collection that already has entries. Meanwhile, small sources of 8 or fewer entries that go into an empty collection continue to use plain conj, because the overhead of buffering would end up costing more than it actually saves. With these changes in place, the worst remaining case ends up being a 4 entry map at 1.05x, which is effectively as good as a red-black tree.

So, now that we've discussed how B+trees work, and what makes them a good alternative to red-black trees in this scenario, let's look at some actual benchmark numbers comparing the two approaches. The numbers were measured using optimized binaries across several runs on an M1 Max with 64 GB. The JVM comparisons use Clojure 1.12.6 on OpenJDK 20. A ratio under 1.0 means the B+tree is faster.

Times are for the whole operation over the collection, which includes building it, doing a lookup for every key, removing every key, and replacing every value. Keys are also scrambled to avoid a degenerate sequential case.

As we can see, lookups win at every size, by 23 to 33%. Builds and writes stay flat below 64 entries. Notably, even a 4 entry map ends up being a single leaf searched in place, meaning that it doesn't pay for the extra machinery.

The reduce-kv result stands out because it's a result of a fix in the new layout. The original red-black tree code built a map entry for every pair going through the generic sequence path. Walking the leaves and passing each key/value pair straight to the function avoids having to allocate memory for each slot. And since the B+tree can seek to a key to start reading from that leaf without having to rebuild a stack of nodes from the root on every call, repeatedly taking the first element of a subseq gets faster as well.

From here on out we hit a cliff where the cache matters more than anything else.

While performance looked good for thousands of elements, it was also important to check what would happen with collections having millions of entries in order to make sure nothing broke or regressed badly at this scale. The following benchmark builds a sorted map and a sorted set from scrambled keys and then runs a mix of operations over them.

And the good news is that every operation at this scale is also faster than the previous version. Not only that, but Jolt is now faster than the JVM at building sets, walking, reducing, and range queries, while the two are roughly even on contains? and the map build. Finally, point lookups and deletes are still about 1.5x slower than the JVM, which uses a red-black tree backed PersistentTreeMap thanks to the magic of the highly optimized JIT that the JVM enjoys.

Peak resident memory for the 4M run nearly halved, going from 1.73 GB to 1.04 GB with the B+tree. It's worth noting that the process holds a 4M entry map with its 4M entry set, along with the garbage from building them. So, the numbers here reflect the whole program rather than just the trees themselves. And the JVM run peaked at 4 to 6 GB, but that's mostly an artifact of how the JVM collects garbage with its default settings, so we shouldn't read too much into that.

You might have noticed that the scrambled builds slow down sharply somewhere between 1M and 2M entries. The JVM also shows the same jump with its sort going from 16 to 93 ms. In both cases, the cause is that the working set ends up falling out of cache, making lookup more expensive.

As I mentioned earlier, Jolt's TreeMap and TreeSet shims are built on the sorted map. These were implemented using a naive approach where they went through it one generic operation at a time. Each put looked up the key and then inserted it, having to walk the tree twice, while navigation methods like floorKey built a subseq and took its first element.

Now, all of these operations have been updated to use the tree directly, meaning that a put or remove is one walk, while operations like floorKey are a single seek. The size of a bounded view can now be computed by adding up whole leaves and only scanning the two partial leaves at the edges. Times are for 20,000 operations.

That's 4 to 70 times faster than the original version, with headMap size beating the JVM, which needs to walk the view in order to count it. But the writes are still about 4x the JVM, and can't be closed with this design because the Java mutates its nodes in place, while Jolt's TreeMap is a mutable wrapper around a persistent tree. So, there's no way around each put having to copy about five nodes.

Iteration order, which key is kept on a duplicate, which value wins, the argument order passed to custom comparators, and returning the identical collection from a no-op assoc all work as they did before. But there is one thing that's different from the JVM, which stems from the layout of the trees. Building a 1,024 entry map from ascending keys now calls the comparator 1,023 times while the JVM's red-black tree calls it 12,301 times. So, code that counts comparator calls will see different numbers on Jolt.

What this exercise shows is the importance of the memory layout used by the backing data structure. All the operations do the same logical work as before, but they now have to touch about a fifth as many nodes with the data inside each node being contiguous.

Switching to use a B+tree was not a free win, though, since it required a separate batch build path to make the switch efficient for code that builds lots of medium-sized maps, which adds some complexity to the implementation. If you're making a similar kind of optimization, always be sure to measure the middle sizes along with the extremes.

#9731. How Security Vendors Are Tackling Access-Control Challenges for AI Agents

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Identity, runtime, and development controls are converging as enterprises look for ways to keep agents within their assigned tasks. But vendors' approaches vary, so CISOs face a choice.

As organizations expand their use of artificial intelligence (AI) agents to perform tasks traditionally done by employees, security teams must control not only which systems agents can access but which actions they are authorized to take.

The Blueprint Alliance, an industry group advocating for coordinated controls, notes that 92% of organizations use autonomous AI agents, but only 34% secure them with the same rigor as they do for human users.

Many vendors have begun adding capabilities to better control agents. Their approaches overlap, leaving CISOs to determine how the new offerings fit into a coherent security architecture that keeps agents focused on their assigned tasks and prevents overpermissioning machine identities beyond what their human users can access.

Earlier this month, CrowdStrike introduced what it calls an AI Kill Switch, which gives security teams a way to block an agent's access to AI models via connected gateways. The AI Kill Switch, launched during CrowdStrike's Fal.Con Europe conference in Barcelona, extends Falcon Guardian, the AI detection and response offering that supports Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints. Guardian discovers agents and controls which ones may run and connects prompts, identities, tool calls, and skills to downstream actions in an execution graph.

Related:Phishing-Resistant Isn't Enough; Yubico Takes Aim at Identity-Verification Gap

The kill switch works with CrowdStrike's Falcon AI Gateway or connected third-party gateways. Its current enforcement point is model access, rather than every system an agent can reach. CrowdStrike says it will later extend the capability to terminate agent processes and revoke their access to enterprise resources.

"The hardest case is the agent that behaves abnormally without breaking a business process rule," CrowdStrike's chief product officer AJ Shipley said during an Oct. 29 media roundtable discussion.

Discussing agent insider threat detection, Shipley described an approach that establishes a baseline of expected agent and user behavior and then detects deviations, even when no explicit policy violation occurs.

CrowdStrike also announced earlier this month agreements to acquire two startups — Fiddler AI and Dreadnode — extending its push into agent observability and predeployment security testing. Fiddler evaluates agents and helps explain their behavior in production, while Dreadnode tests models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment. The Wall Street Journal reported a combined purchase price of approximately $495 million. The acquisitions have not yet closed.

Related:Cyera's Oasis Security Buy Is All About AI Agent Control

CrowdStrike is one of several vendors addressing agent access controls. Anaconda is combining agentic software development with autonomous security testing, Cisco and Teleport are tying access to infrastructure identity, Okta is enforcing identity policy when agents call tools, and Fortinet is extending controls over execution and application behavior.

Anaconda, for instance, is approaching the problem through application development by pairing agentic software development with autonomous security testing. Last month, it expanded its AI Dev Factory, combining development agent swarms with autonomous red-team agents that probe models, agents, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for weaknesses. The release incorporates technology from Anaconda's August acquisition of Enkrypt AI, supporting red teaming across more than 300 attack categories and runtime guardrails that approve, modify, or block risky behavior.

Anaconda's earlier acquisitions of Outerbounds, Kilo Code, and Enkrypt AI collectively bring together production orchestration, agentic development, and AI security.

"Our road map out for all three acquisitions would have been about two or three years’ worth of engineering effort," Anaconda CEO David DeSanto says, describing Enkrypt as the final component needed to accomplish this goal.

Related:USA Fencing Lunges Into the Hidden Identity Challenge in Amateur Sports

Testing agents is one requirement; limiting their authority in production is another. Cisco is approaching that problem through infrastructure identity, becoming Teleport's largest strategic investor in August. Teleport's open source platform replaces passwords and permanent SSH keys with ephemeral certificates.

Teleport CEO Ev Kontsevoy describes an incident in which a customer deployed an agent to process data and update a database. When the intended database became unavailable, the agent found another and tried to update it. The agent was trying to complete its assignment rather than respond to an attacker. Its improvisation nevertheless exposed the difference between granting access and containing behavior.

"Would you say it's a security accident or what? Whatever it is, it's terrifying when it happens, particularly at scale," Kontsevoy tells Dark Reading.

Cisco and Teleport's partnership addresses containment through verified infrastructure identities and access granted "just in time, just enough," says Peter Bailey, Cisco's senior VP and general manager for security.

"We want to be able to take action and stop action based upon identity," Bailey says.

On Oct. 26, Cisco introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, applying the partnership's infrastructure-identity approach to administrators and agents. Cisco says it provides temporary, identity-bound access to network infrastructure, records sessions, and ends privileges when the task is complete.

Kontsevoy describes attaching privileges to tasks rather than permanently assigning them to accounts. A deployment ticket could identify the engineer, laptop, and CI/CD pipeline involved. Each is granted necessary privileges, which disappear when the ticket closes. Teleport's MCP gateway also enforces policy and tracks relationships among initiating actors, agents, and subagents, he says.

When an agent acts on an employee's behalf, controls must distinguish the agent's permissions from those of the person directing the agent to avoid inappropriate privilege escalation.

Consider a scenario in which an HR assistant runs on a service account that can read every employee record. A contractor asking the agent for the CEO's compensation could get the response since the assistant has access the contractor doesn't. According to Okta, this agent would be a "confused deputy," as it exercises authority the requester lacks.

To address this scenario, Okta's Agent Gateway treats agents as "first-class" identities; it preserves the distinction between their permissions and those of the users directing them. It requires a credential that identifies both the user and the agent and uses token exchange to preserve the delegation context. The gateway limits the tools available, while the downstream MCP server enforces the user's record-level access. Agent Gateway is now generally available as an addition to AI agents, an identity-security offering made generally available in April.

In an Oct. 8 blog post, Okta described plans for Cross App Access support and a gateway-based kill switch. Officials said the latter "will make agent deactivation immediate, down to tokens already issued, by rejecting any request carrying a token issued to a deactivated agent."

Okta is not alone in extending identity controls to agents. At its Fal.Con conference in Las Vegas in September, CrowdStrike announced Agentic Identity Provider, designed to establish trusted agent identities, broker time-limited access, and link actions to initiating employees or systems.

Microsoft is pursuing a related approach through Project Perception, connecting agent identity, behavioral risk signals, and access controls across its security products via its new Guardian Agent capabilities.

Meanwhile, Fortinet is extending AI inspection across its existing network security products. Last month, the company announced the FortiGuard Inline AI Security Service for FortiGate customers and described expanded FortiAIGate capabilities incorporating Virtue AI technology, which Fortinet acquired earlier this year. Virtue AI adds policy-derived guardrails, continuous assessment, code analysis, and agent red teaming.

Fortinet executive vice president Anthony James describes more than 50 simulated application environments in which customers can test agent boundaries before connecting to real systems. He says Virtue can block an agent from communicating with MCP tools or servers not approved for its task and detect prompt sequences that progress from innocuous to malicious.

FortiAIGate began by monitoring communications to and from AI infrastructure, James adds. Customers deploying agents sought a deeper understanding of the application. Models, MCP servers, agents, and skills "require a little deeper application knowledge than just interpreting the network traffic," he says.

Overlapping approaches have prompted coordination efforts. In September, Okta announced the Blueprint Alliance with vendors including AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler. The group aims to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors' products.

The alliance has outlined principles for agent identity, task-scoped access, monitoring, and containment. Whether those principles translate into interoperable products and expanded adoption remains to be seen.

Taken together, these approaches point to a common requirement: keeping an agent's access tied to its assigned task. Identity verification, security testing, and runtime monitoring address different parts of that requirement, but no single control confirms that an agent will remain within its assignment.

Emerging control planes aim to connect those controls across tools and systems — limiting agents to their assigned tasks rather than letting AI software determine how far its authority extends.

#9730. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

CachyOS, a performance-focused distribution based on Arch Linux, has announced its November 2026 release. Notable changes in this release include a new recovery environment ("cachyos-recovery") for rolling back broken systems, Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) v2 support for games that require EAC to run, version 2.0.0 of the CachyOS Package Installer, and more.

1. DRM and anticheat are, to a large part, one and the same, including that they're trying to best-effort solve a theoretically impossible problem by locking down clients.

Not purchasing DRM-requiring games is really the best way to do this. Until then, refuse to help deploy such mechanisms (can't really not help with implementation unless you also think that no one should be able to do lockdown-like things to their own hardware or avoiding contributing to any such thing). Game studios certainly have the right to release games that require it. It's just better if no one buys them then.

After that came Secure Boot, which when enabled (and the security hysteria is that you must always have it enabled, even though its driving use case of "not allowing any untrusted code to run before the antivirus starts" is not very relevant for Linux) makes it harder to use a self-compiled kernel. It seems that, outside of source-focused distributions, we've grown complacent and got too comfortable letting someone else compile the software we use. Quick question: can you, with a single command, download and rebuild any package of your favorite distribution (in a way which allows easily applying local changes to it), or does it require deep developer knowlege and a bunch of esoteric commands with a long list of magic options?

#9728. UQ researchers send an unblockable message using gravity

Professor Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Professor Andrew White inside the elevator they used to send a message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland. )

University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter.

The unusual experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between 2 levels, moving its 1.8-tonne counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, ‘Gravity’.

Dr Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics said gravitational communication had an intriguing advantage.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” Dr Woffinden said.

“Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”

Dr Andrew Groszek said the idea came from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr Groszek said.

“Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realised the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”

Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White said.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field from the elevator's movement and translated the message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland.)

Professor Matthew Davis said the UQ team had established an important underlying principle.

“It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating,” Professor Davis said.

“We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modelling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 metres and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”

Such sensors could eventually support communication in environments where radio waves, light and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

Read the research published in Science Advances.

This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive.

Oracle has released versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 11.0.33.0.3 and 8u511b3 of the JDK as part of their quarterly Critical Security Patch Update Advisory for November 2026. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.1.0.3, version 25.0.5.0.3, version 21.0.13.0.3, version 17.0.21.0.3, version 11.0.33.0.3 and version 8u511 b33.

JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.

JEP 548, Vector API (Thirteenth Incubator), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8397768 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a thirteenth incubation with one notable change, after twelve rounds of incubation delivered in JDK 16 through JDK 27. This feature introduces an API to "express vector computations that reliably compile at runtime to optimal vector instructions on supported CPU architectures, thus achieving performance superior to equivalent scalar computations." This JEP adds support for Vector vectors, whose lanes hold 16-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 binary16 format. The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. At that time, the Vector API team will adapt the Vector API and its implementation to use them, and will promote the Vector API from Incubation to Preview.

Build 25 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 24 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

A new Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), affects versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3 and 8u511b33-perf of Oracle Java SE, versions 21.0.13.0.3 and 17.0.21.0.3 of Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. As described in the CVE documentation:

[This] difficult to exploit vulnerability allows [an] unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.

Organizations and projects that have addressed this CVE include: BellSoft, Azul, JetBrains, GraalVM, Quarkus and WildFly. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

It was a busy week over at Spring as the various teams have delivered GA releases that include: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Security, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOAS, Spring Modulith, Spring AI, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring LDAP.

The Spring team has also resolved a total of 90 CVEs spanning multiple projects. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

The release of Azul Payara 7.6.0, the November 2026 edition, includes Community Edition 7.2026.11, Enterprise Edition 6.44.0 and Enterprise Edition 5.93.0. Along with bug fixes and component upgrades, all three editions deliver resolutions to five CVEs, two of which are related to Azul Payara:

Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and the Azul Payara security advisories page.

The second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 ship with one single bug fix from the first release candidates, in which use of the Jakarta Persistence @TableGenerator annotation could cause a deadlock when a session holding the lock on the row of the generator table needed a new block of IDs.

Version 5.0.0.CR2 will be the last release candidate. With the GA release of version 5.0.0.Final, it will be declared as end-of-life and focus will be on version 5.1.0.

More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR2 and version 5.0.0.CR2.

The release of Java Operator SDK 5.7.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to enable virtual threads via construction in the Operator class or the josdk.use-virtual-threads property; and a new keepAlive() method, defined in the Operator class that starts a non-daemon thread to keep the JVM running until the operator is shut down. Version 5.7 is now built on Fabric8 Kubernetes Client 8.0. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) for November 2026, BellSoft has released CSPU patches for versions 27.0.1.1 25.0.5.1, 21.0.13.1, 17.0.21.1, 11.0.33.1, 8u514 7u523 and 6u523 of Liberica JDK, their downstream distribution of OpenJDK, to address this list of CVEs. This release also includes a patch for the aforementioned Java4Shell Remote Code Execution vulnerability.

With an overall total of 111 fixes and backports, BellSoft states they have participated in eliminating 21 issues in all releases.

The release of Helidon 27.0.2 delivers bug fixes and one notable change in which the default limit of decoded-input (strings, byte arrays, JSON, forms, and buffered multipart parts) for in-memory entity conversations has been increased to 1 mebibyte (MiB). More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

This release also aligns with the Oracle Critical Patch Updates for November 2026 and includes the Helidon 4.x and 3.x release trains as described in this blog post.

The formal release (along with the thirty-fourth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.24.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new DecisionSchedulerPlanner and DecisionModels classes to serve as a decision model-based agentic pattern; and support for resuming suspended agentic systems in the AgentMonitor class. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes.

After two milestones and two releases candidates, the GA release of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: an optimization of the PrometheusMeterRegistry and MicrometerCollector classes for collecting data snapshots; and a new RowState inner class, defined in the MultiGauge class, that eliminates the need to remove and re-register an instance of the existing Row inner class. More details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

Similarly, the GA release of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a simplification of baggage handles and lookups by directly storing the name of the handle and its metadata by eliminating use of the CompositeBaggage and Java AtomicReference classes; and a refactor of the BaggageTextMapPropagator class for improved baggage propagation. Further details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.
