#9726. Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the hf cli like so:

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Show interactive benchmark results with downloadable data

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

#9725. Sneakernet

NOTICE: Sneakernet is a work in progress. The documentation makes some promises that are not reflected in the current state of affairs. Links to to-be-written parts of the documentation are indicated in red.

Sneakernet is a system for securely1 sending digital messages to other people without using the Internet. Instead, messages are automatically passed on to other Sneakernet users on your local network – at your hackerspace, an event or conference, your local cafe, etc — and then physically carried to their destination on your “sneakers”, where they will be automatically delivered to any recipients on the same network (or handed over to be carried further on by someone else).

Sneakernet encourages slow, thoughtful participation in community and face-to-face meetings with the users who will carry your messages onwards to their destination, and entrust their own messages to you.

⇒ Head to Getting started to set up Sneakernet on your device.

Many applications can be built on top of sneakernet’s general-purpose messaging system, provided that they are tolerant of high latency and out-of-order messages. Some examples include:

Building your own sneakernet applications is easy, too, in any programming language – see Building applications for more details.

All messages are authenticated and all private messages are also encrypted. People who carry your messages along cannot tamper with them and cannot read your private messages. See Security for more details.

#9723. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

hi, which models are supported with this? is mobernbert and t5gemma2 on the list?

Hi, we now have a space where you can chek if a model is supported: https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support

#9720. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9718. AI Agents Zip From Flaw Discovery to Root Access in 11 Minutes

A China-nexus actor used the Cairn penetration testing tool in attacks against East Asian universities, exploiting a zero-day in a medical imaging app.

A China-linked threat actor went from discovering a vulnerability in an application to gaining root access to the server it was running on in about 11 minutes, using Cairn AI agents. The incident, uncovered by researchers at Amazon Threat Intelligence, offers yet another example of how quickly attackers can optimize their operations using AI.

The campaign, which ran for approximately 48 hours beginning Sept. 8, targeted universities across East Asia outside mainland China, with probing and reconnaissance aimed at taking control of IT systems, according to a report published Friday by Amazon Threat Intelligence.

"The actor gave the agents a simple goal: 'obtain shell access,'" CJ Moses, chief information security officer (CISO) of Amazon Web Services (AWS), wrote in the report. During the campaign, the agents discovered a zero-day in an exposed open source medical imaging application and used it to gain full control of a server in about 11 minutes.

Related:China's 'Armory Castle' Lays Siege to VMware vCenter Zero-Day

"These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable," he wrote.

The revelation follows reports of other China-linked actors using Cairn-based AI agents in various attacks, including breaching 10 organizations to steal secrets and automating a massive attack spree against high-profile websites. Cairn is an open source, AI-based penetration testing tool that threat actors are using, along with a similar tool called Artex, to facilitate and automate their cyberattacks.

In this case, the AI agents conducted two extensive operations that failed before they found and exploited the zero-day, demonstrating their adaptability and persistence even without human direction, Moses said.

The most comprehensive unsuccessful operation involved attempts to take control of a Redis instance at one university that was configured to allow unauthenticated access. The effort lasted about 16 hours and involved 148 sequential actions. Along the way, the agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an exposed Redis server and also attempted Log4Shell injection against another service running on the same system.

A separate operation lasted more than six hours and targeted a university GPU server. The agents began with a list of about 80 real usernames, which they assembled by researching the university's public presence.

Using those names, they unsuccessfully tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against the server's remote login service (SSH). They also attempted access to an admin dashboard, network storage device, VPN server, and campus portal across the university network.

Related:Nok et norsk energiselskap har blitt utsatt for et datainnbrudd på to dager

"Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses observed in the post.

The agents eventually succeeded against a target running an open source medical imaging AI application. They first identified the application's framework and mapped its API endpoints, finding an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. When they tested the parameter for path traversal, they scored their first win: The endpoint was vulnerable, Moses said.

"In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application's API to arbitrarily writing files on the server," he wrote. The agents then used the same vulnerability to execute a Python reverse shell payload as root on the compromised server.

There's been plenty of discussion about how AI agents operate at "machine speed," taking far less time than humans to find and exploit flaws. But in this case, the speed at which the agents found the vulnerability isn't what's most impressive in 2026, says Cris Thomas, a former hacker with the L0pht Heavy Industries collective and current security advocate at security platform provider Semgrep.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

That would be the case "if it was 2017," he says. What's notable instead is that AI agents are doing this without a skilled human involved. That "changes the economics of vulnerability discovery, and defenders need to take advantage of the same technology," Thomas observes.

"Attackers are getting faster, but the answer isn't to abandon the fundamentals; it is to double down on them," he says. "They are fundamental for a reason."

Those fundamentals include monitoring for suspicious uploads, unexpected file writes, and unusual process execution, as well as reviewing code as it's written, Thomas says. "[These are] the same things we should have been doing for decades, only now a whole lot faster," he notes.

Just as AI agents operate at machine speed, "defenders need to make those fundamentals work at machine speed, with automated detection and containment backed by human oversight for consequential decisions," Thomas advises.

Another defense against AI-driven attacks is "continuously analyzing server logs, [which] helps IT teams learn what normal activity looks like and spot unusual patterns that could signal an attack in progress," says Ross Filipek, CISO at cybersecurity consulting firm Corsica Technologies.

Given that the agents targeted exposed endpoints and servers, Filipek also recommends that organizations maintain an inventory of exposed assets, restrict access to applications that only staff need, and decide in advance who has authority to isolate a server after hours.

"That's a decision you want settled before the alert comes in," Filipek says.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

InfoQ Homepage News JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28

Nov 23, 2026 4 min read

JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving the work of acquiring and preparing heap memory off the startup path and onto dedicated concurrent worker threads. On Linux 6.1 and later it also upgrades 4 KB pages to 2 MB pages while the application runs. The 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's headline numbers comes from elsewhere: adaptive heap sizing, in the companion JEP 546, which still defaults to off.

Deploying ZGC has until now meant choosing which half of a trade-off to pay for. The collector's pause times do not grow with the heap, but its collection frequency does, so a small heap brings on early and frequent cycles. The JEP describes the older ergonomic behavior of committing one sixty-fourth of physical memory for the initial heap.

A team chasing fast startup set a tiny -Xms and accepted a long warmup, because the collector then had to acquire and prepare memory in increments while the application was already allocating. A team chasing fast warmup set a large -Xms, usually with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, and paid the whole bill before the first request landed. The JEP puts the spread at roughly a tenth of a second to start with a 2 MB heap against more than ten seconds with a 32 GB one on current hardware.

That work now happens in a new thread, ZMemoryWorker, one per heap partition. It commits and uncommits memory concurrently as capacity changes. It also heats memory before application threads reach it, which means pre-touching page by page and collapsing small pages into large ones.

The budget is fixed rather than adaptive. ZConcurrentWorkersCPUShare in zGlobals.hpp is 0.25, so preparation takes at most a quarter of the available CPU. ZGC's director caps young-generation worker counts when adaptive sizing is on, which keeps collection inside its CPU target while expansion continues and the collector deliberately runs above its heuristic heap size target.

Large pages on Linux no longer require an administrator to reserve them up front. ZGC probes for MADV_COLLAPSE, the madvise mode added in Linux 6.1, by mapping a 4 MB region, pre-touching a single page and collapsing an aligned 2 MB range. When the probe succeeds and memory heating is enabled, the collector enters a new Collapse state and upgrades pages in the background. The call races the kernel's khugepaged, so the implementation retries on EAGAIN.

The change shows up in what a deployer no longer has to decide. Where JDK 25 forced a choice between two tunings, JDK 28 offers a third option:

The third command produces the JEP's case study figures, a 38% drop in startup time and a fall in warmup from 80 seconds to 10 for Spring PetClinic on a 32 GB machine. -XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing takes the minimum and initial heap down to 2 MB and raises the MaxHeapSize ceiling to 100% of physical memory. Without it, ZGC falls back to the shared heap sizing path and a 25% ceiling. Concurrent preparation still runs, but not the aggressive expansion the measurements depend on.

Using identical memory techniques on every operating system is an explicit non-goal, so large pages may be the default on Linux and not on Windows. The JEP also cautions that applications tuned around a larger initial heap may warm up more slowly and need re-tuning.

Two further edges live in the implementation rather than the text. Pairing -XX:+UseLargePages with adaptive sizing and no -Xmx logs a warning and disables explicit large pages for the heap. The retry loop around MADV_COLLAPSE can also spin indefinitely when EAGAIN persists, a case the code attributes to pinning through mlock or long-term DMA and treats as user error.

Teams can see the heap sizing difference for themselves on the JDK 28 early-access builds by comparing the resolved flags:

The second run drops the minimum and initial sizes to the 2 MB floor and lifts the maximum from a quarter of physical memory to all of it. Adding -Xlog:gc+init reports Memory Heating: Enabled and, once the collapse path is active, Large Page Support: Enabled (Transparent, JVM enforced).

Services already running a modest heap on Linux 6.1 or later pick up concurrent pre-touch and background large pages without touching a flag, because memory heating is on by default. Services carrying a large pre-touched heap purely to buy warmup have something to delete, though only after enabling adaptive sizing. That 100% ceiling reads worse than it behaves. The policy tracks machine-wide memory and holds a reserve, preferring to leave a fifth of the machine free, fighting for a tenth and enforcing a twentieth, with those margins widening when usage is unstable or compressed.

JDK 28 reaches Rampdown Phase One on December 3, 2026, with general availability scheduled for March 9, 2027. The JEP's own future work points at better CPU sharing between concurrent collection and concurrent commit, and at ahead-of-time compilation from JEP 544, already Completed for JDK 28, which frees JIT cycles the memory workers could spend instead.

#9716. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9714. Quality IMAP, Part 2: Mailbox Concurrency

In the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the second part in a series discussing why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and presenting our work on making Aerogramme's IMAP code as high-quality as we can. Today we focus on challenges that arise when considering concurrent access to a mailbox.

Aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network issues and hardware failures. It is built on top of Garage and shares the same philosophy. Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building.

This is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy, essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement. In the previous post, we talked about the first class of features: fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents. In this post, we talk about the second class of features that make implementing an IMAP server tricky: concurrent access to user mailboxes.

Concurrent and distributed software are famously hard to get right; concurrency bugs are known to be hard to find. In our recent work on refining Aerogramme we have tried to approach the problem from different angles. This is the topic of this post: the different ways in which we have improved the correctness of Aerogramme in concurrent settings.

This work was funded by NLNet under the "Aerogramme 1.0" grant, and could not have been possible without their support.

Feel free to join the Aerogramme matrix channel for updates or if you just want to chat!

A core feature of IMAP is that multiple email clients can simultaneously access the same mailbox. For example, we may want to access our emails both from our phone and our computer. Concurrent access to a mailbox can also happen when a single client is involved: some clients (including Thunderbird) open multiple concurrent connections to a same mailbox to speed up processing. In any case, clients accessing the same mailbox should be able to coordinate between themselves and avoid stepping on each other's toes.

Why must clients be able to coordinate when accessing the same mailbox? Assume that we are an email client that sends two commands to read information from a mailbox. Since another client can modify the mailbox in between the two commands, the information we read may have been invalidated by the other client and is now inconsistent! Clients thus need to be able to detect concurrent changes made by other clients. Similarly, a client that reconnects to the server after being offline needs to fetch the changes that happened while it was disconnected. This is possible thanks to mechanisms defined by the IMAP specification and that specifically exist because concurrent access is allowed.

The overall consistency of the mailbox data must be taken seriously: an IMAP server exposing inconsistent views of a mailbox could result in a confused client deleting the wrong emails, for example.

To our best knowledge, concurrent mailbox behaviors are tackled in the following (parts of) specifications:

The base IMAP4 specification has few explicit mentions of concurrent mailbox access, but does talk about re-synchronizing disconnected clients, which can be seen as a restricted form of concurrent access. It defines mechanisms for assigning IDs to emails (UIDNEXT/UIDVALIDITY) and associated properties which can be extrapolated to concurrent contexts. This is relevant when concurrently adding new emails to a mailbox. After an email has been added to a mailbox it cannot be modified, so there are no issues with reading emails concurrently.

The improvements that we will talk about in this post are related to these aspects of the base IMAP specification.

As an additional complication, IMAP defines in fact two (!) email-numbering systems. One of these has the drawback that deleting an email can invalidate email IDs used in concurrent commands. This is purely a quirk of a numbering system that can nowadays be considered legacy, but must still be supported. This issue is not acknowledged in the base IMAP specification, leaving a class of problematic behaviors completely unspecified, but is later addressed in an informational RFC which specifies what to do in such cases.

Aerogramme's latest release includes changes and bugfixes to make sure that we follow the recommendations of this informational RFC, but we won't enter into the details of these legacy quirks in this post.

Email flags can be modified concurrently, but the base IMAP specification does not specify a mechanism for clients to coordinate around flag changes. This is done in the later CONDSTORE specification that extends IMAP with mechanisms to coordinate flag changes across concurrent connections. Aerogramme has preliminary support for CONDSTORE, but we disabled it in the last release, as we found out it needs a redesign to be nicer to email clients1.

A later specification further extends IMAP and CONDSTORE by adding a more general mechanism (QRESYNC) for synchronizing all mailbox changes across concurrent sessions. Aerogramme does not supports QRESYNC at the moment2.

On top of the complexity carried by the IMAP specification, Aerogramme's distributed infrastructure comes with its own challenges. Not only we need to think about concurrency at the IMAP protocol level, but also internally in Aerogramme: how do we handle concurrent changes to the server internal data storage? Can we simply take a lock or a transaction over mailbox data each time we need to update it, serializing all concurrent updates? The answer is no: things are a bit more complicated...

Recall that Aerogramme is a distributed IMAP server. A typical Aerogramme deployment looks like this:

In this schema, A nodes are Aerogramme instances running on separate servers. Running multiple Aerogramme nodes provides fault-tolerance: even if some of the nodes crash, the Aerogramme cluster stays operational as long as one node remains available. When an email client (a C node) connects to the "Aerogramme cluster" (the dashed potato), it can open a connection to any of the Aerogramme nodes, depending on what kind of load-balancing is implemented.

Aerogramme nodes do not talk to each other directly and do not store data themselves. Instead, they connect a shared Garage cluster (itself geo-distributed with fault-tolerance properties) which stores data for the whole Aerogramme cluster (emails, mailbox state, etc.).

This means that an Aerogramme node deals with concurrency at two levels. It must handle concurrent connections from email clients to a mailbox, as we explained before. But it must also handle concurrent changes made by other Aerogramme nodes to the data stored in Garage. These concurrent accesses must be coordinated properly so that the Aerogramme cluster exposes a consistent view of a mailbox (according to IMAP's consistency requirements), even when connecting concurrently to different nodes of the Aerogramme cluster.

A central challenge in Aerogramme's design is that Garage does not provide locks, transactions, or anything that would require distributed consensus between Garage nodes. This is by design, and it allows Garage and Aerogramme to perform well even with non-negligible latency between nodes. The consequence for Aerogramme is that its nodes cannot simply reason on their shared data as if it was updated sequentially. The approach used by Aerogramme insteadâa convergent operation logâis a central part of its design. We'll talk more below on how we adjusted the consistency properties provided by Garage when storing that operation log.

A basic IMAP mechanism is assigning IDs to emails when they are added into a mailbox. Adding emails concurrently can already make it tricky to assign these IDs. Our first step was to find a way of testing this case and to fix any bugs that we would find.

For context, IMAP specifies that each email in a mailbox must be assigned a UID: a number that identifies it uniquely. UIDs are assigned in increasing order; this allows clients to check if new emails have been added by checking the value of the mailbox "next UID". On top of that, IMAP also allows the server to renumber the emails with different UIDs. When this happens, the IMAP server must increase the value of UIDVALIDITY, a global integer counter attached to the mailbox. Now, in Aerogramme, increasing UIDVALIDITY is done in some cases when emails are added concurrently in the mailbox in a way that would assign conflicting UIDs; an unavoidable consequence of its distributed architecture.

From an IMAP client's perspective UIDVALIDITY must always increase monotonically. We also assume that this property must hold across all concurrent connections; although the specification does not say so explicitly, it is the most prudent assumption since a single client may open multiple connections to the same mailbox.

The logical next step is to setup a test bench to ensure that it holds in practice for Aerogramme! We deployed an Aerogramme cluster with three nodes, running on a simulated network with added latency between nodes. Then:

Running Aerogramme on this test bench found state synchronization bugs: bugs showing that Aerogrammeâs distributed state (stored in Garage) was not always properly synchronized between nodes and concurrent sessions. Amusingly, most of these bugs were not specific to the IMAP logic related to UIDVALIDITY...

Fixing these synchronization bugs motivated a redesign of the internal read/update mailbox interface. In Aerogramme, the IMAP "business logic" accesses mailbox state stored in distributed storage using an abstract interface exposing a small number of operations. Before, these operations were the following (in pseudo-Rust):

The synchronization bugs found during testing revealed that this interface is in fact error-prone and tricky to reason about:

The solution was to redesign Aerogramme's mailbox state interface to provide more control over state synchronization: reading concurrent changes from storage becomes a separate operation, laying the following interface:

This new interface separates local reasoning about mailbox contents from synchronization. This makes it easier to write the IMAP logic in a way that is "obviously correct". Plainly speaking, this interface provides "local" views of mailbox state, where a view (denoted as self above) is specific to a client connection. Then, get and push_op operate on the local view with sequential semantics and are both fast; and calls to sync mark explicitly the places in the code where we have to think about concurrent changes. (Note that push_op synchronously updates remote storage, so there is no risk of losing write by forgetting to run sync.)

Notice that the design of this interface reflects the high-level distributed architecture that we described in the previous section. For instance, an implementation of the interface needs to "merge" the operations pushed concurrently with push_op when they are put together in distributed storage, in a way that is consistent with local views; this is backed by the "convergent operation log" mentioned earlier and domain-specific logic3. Note that this interface offers no transactional or lock-like operations; matching Garage's lack of consistency primitives.

Most of the changes described here were part of Aerogramme 0.4, with in particular #129 implementing the refactoring of the state synchronization interface.

Talking about consistency guarantees in Aerogramme raises the question: what are the consistency guarantees provided by Garage, its storage backend?

This question is most relevant for Garage K2V, a NoSQL-inspired key-value store, which is used to store mailbox state as an operation log. (Garage K2V is experimental and was added in Garage for the needs of Aerogramme.) Mailbox state describes (among other things) email numbering, and as we've seen before, we want this information to be properly synchronized between Aerogramme nodes.

Garage K2V provides read-after-write consistency4: this guarantees that as soon as a write is acknowledged by Garage, any subsequent read will see the update made by the write. In terms of Aerogramme's state synchronization interface, after running push_op(op);, this guarantees that sync(); get() returns a state that includes op on any Aerogramme node.

However, it turns out that read-after-write consistency alone is not enough for Aerogramme. Let's think of the fact that UIDVALIDITY needs to increase monotonically according to the IMAP specification. This means that calling sync(); get() twice on any two Aerogramme nodes must return a state that is more recent the second time than the first. In other words, when making several reads to Garage K2V in sequence, we must not see time go backward. This means that, to ensure consistency of the UIDVALIDITY counter, Aerogramme needs Garage K2V to guarantee an additional consistency property called monotonic reads!

As a result we have extended Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads consistency. Luckily, the design of Garage makes it possible to provide monotonic reads at only a small performance cost. For a reference, Martin Kleppmann's Designing data-intensive applications (in particular ChapterÂ 9, "Linearizability and quorums") helps understanding which scenarios lead to non-monotonic reads in a quorum-based architecture like Garage's, and what to implement to guarantee monotonic reads.

To experimentally validate our changes, we first built a test bench that triggers non-monotonic reads on stock K2V. Reproducing non-monotonic reads requires variable network delays, so we deployed a Garage cluster with 3 nodes, on a simulated network with delay between cluster nodes. This test setup allows observing non-monotonic reads, by running:

We then modified Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads by default, by implementing "synchronous read repair". We validated that we cannot observe non-monotonic reads anymore on our test bench, while they could be observed before this change: a good sanity check.

This change in Garage K2V ensures that there are no scenarios in which a precise combination of network delays in the cluster results in an IMAP client observing non-increasing values of UIDVALIDITY. One could argue that this is unlikely to happen in practice; and indeed, we could not reproduce it with our simple-minded test bench: while we could observe non-monotonic reads with Garage K2V alone, we could not observe non-monotonic UIDVALIDITY on a full Garage+Aerogramme deployment with the same testing methodology. Nevertheless, we want Aerogramme to rest on strong, correct foundations as much as possible; eliminating a rare but possible cause of bugs was fully worth the effort.

The work described here was made available as part of Garage 2.4.0; it required no specific change in Aerogramme itself.

We designed Aerogramme to be part of a low-tech computing stack meant to be robust and reliable when hosted outside of data-centers, and Aerogramme's geo-distributed design is part of the answer. In the future, we hope to expand on the values and high-level ideas behind Aerogramme; this will have to be for an other blogpost...

The current implementation (now gated by a feature flag disabled by default) tends to disconnect clients more often than reasonable. This is correct with respect to the specification, but likely leads to bad UX in clients. We are working on a better strategy that does not require disconnecting clients.

The first step would be to gather data on how many clients actually support QRESYNC today...

We have not shown this "domain specific" merge logic (here, mailbox-specific) because it is a whole different topic, but it needs to be provided when instantiating the generic interface shown before with concrete state and operations.

read-after-write consistency is also the key consistency guarantee provided by Garage S3.

#9712. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9709. Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!
