#9671. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9670. US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

Trump named Kirsten Davies as Acting National Cyber Director, bringing greater industry experience to the role amid recent outages and rising geopolitical tensions.

The Office of the National Cyber Director will have a new, more technically experienced director at the helm, but how that might impact US cyber policy remains to be seen.

President Donald Trump on Nov. 19 tapped Kirsten Davies to lead the White House Office of the National Cyber Director, replacing Sean Cairncross, who is leaving the administration. Last December, Davies was appointed the chief information officer of the Department of Defense.

In a Nov. 20 news release, the White House said Davies "will drive an America First cyber strategy that treats cybersecurity as national security and keeps the United States dominant and secure in cyberspace." Upon last Thursday's announcement, Davies became Acting United States National Cyber Director, though she requires Senate confirmation to gain permanent directorship.

In a post on social media platform X, Davies wrote that the US has an opportunity "to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."

Related:Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors

Though not officially tied to Davies' appointment, Cairncross's departure occurred amid a number of outages affecting the public sector. Just this month, there was the outage against the Federal Aviation Administration that lasted for days, as well as an NSA communications network outage that apparently resulted from a software update. Other disruptions hit major banks and Microsoft services.

Melinda Marks, senior research director and chief analyst of cybersecurity at Omdia (an Informa TechTarget property), tells Dark Reading the outages seen in recent weeks have created significant speculation about US security posture. As such, Davies's appointment comes at a time where cybersecurity's role in national security is "more important than ever."

A source close to the White House told Dark Reading sister publication Cybersecurity Dive that Trump fired Cairncross over concerns regarding his cybersecurity credentials; a source told Semafor's Ashley Gold Cairncross resigned of his own volition.

Jacob Krell, senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity at Suzu Labs, tells Dark Reading that Cairncross is primarily an election lawyer who admitted at his June 2025 confirmation hearing that he had no technical background in cyber. Meanwhile, Davies has previously held security leadership roles at Unilever, The Estée Lauder Companies, Barclays, Hewlett-Packard, and Siemens.

Related:In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools, Maybe More

"It is a definite shift from a political appointee to one with much more experience in the industry," he says. "Given the string of massive outages and rising geopolitical tensions, it could not come at a better time."

It remains to be seen how a new National Cyber Director appointment may shape the future of cybersecurity in the US; should she be appointed, Davies stands to have substantial influence, given she would serve as Trump's primary adviser regarding cybersecurity policy and strategy.

Since Trump began his second term at the beginning of 2025, the makeup of US cyber has shifted immensely, between a culling of public sector cyber personnel, a lean into AI technologies, the shuttering of the Cyber Safety Review Board, and more.

Krell says he expects Davies's appointment to potentially shift cyber funding from AI-as-opportunity toward capacity-related expenditures, such as people, test environments, and change control. And as global tensions rise, he expects to see more focus on infrastructure and industrial control systems (ICS).

"Last week showed what machine-speed patching does to human-sized teams," he argues. "AI gets reclassified in the process, from capability accelerator to governed risk."

Related:Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9668. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

#9667. CrowdStrike Makes AI Security Push With Blockbuster Zscaler Deal

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

CrowdStrike's $44 billion acquisition of Zscaler would unite endpoint protection and zero-trust network security to obtain greater control over AI agents.

CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire Zscaler for $43.9 billion in stock, combining endpoint protection and zero-trust network security to help enterprises control AI agents running across their systems.

The deal, announced Monday, aims to give chief information security officers (CISOs) a single supplier for security controls spanning endpoints where agents operate and the network connections used to reach applications and data.

The proposed transaction surpasses Google’s $32 billion acquisition of Wiz, making it the largest announced cybersecurity acquisition on record. For customers, what remains to be seen is whether the companies can turn their existing integrations into unified enforcement while preserving support for competing products.

CrowdStrike co-founder and CEO George Kurtz said the proliferation of AI agents has changed the role of network security, making Zscaler’s traffic inspection complementary to the Falcon platform's visibility into endpoints and cloud workloads.

Related:Microsoft Debuts Offensive, Defensive Security Tools for the AI Era

"The network used to connect people to places," Kurtz said during an investor call announcing the deal and discussing CrowdStrike's fiscal third-quarter results. "Now it connects agents to data."

CrowdStrike expects the transaction to close in the second half of fiscal 2028, subject to customary closing conditions. The companies will operate independently until closing, chief financial officer (CFO) Burt Podbere said.

Bringing network and endpoint security into a common control plane makes sense even without the growth of AI agents, according to cybersecurity analyst Frank Dickson, founder of Dickson Research. Their increasing use makes the combination more compelling, he says.

CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian discovers AI agents, governs their access, and protects them at runtime, Kurtz said. Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange provides inline inspection and access controls for traffic moving to applications and services. Combining those capabilities would connect what an agent does on a device with where it sends data, according to the two companies.

Kurtz described the planned integration with an example of an agent on a laptop pulling sensitive information and sending it to an unapproved AI model. Falcon would see the agent's activity on the device, while Zscaler would see the destination on the network.

"Together, it will be one detection, one decision, and one kill switch that stops the agent on the device and cuts its path on the network," Kurtz said.

Related:Agentic Browsers Rewind Web Security by 20 Years

The companies already share 16 integrations, and customers send Zscaler data into CrowdStrike's Next-Gen SIEM. Kurtz said the combination would bring their telemetry together in that platform and use the expanded dataset to support CrowdStrike's security AI models.

Zscaler founder, chairman, and CEO Jay Chaudhry said combining the companies will allow them to go beyond what they can accomplish through existing partner integrations, including coordinating policy enforcement across endpoints, cloud environments, and the network.

"Imagine being able to have a unified policy that can do all this stuff," Chaudhry said during the conference call.

Dickson says Zscaler's network-centric architecture should make integrating the endpoint software less burdensome than it might seem, because much of Zscaler's processing happens in its distributed network rather than on the device.

"The integration is going to be much lighter because much of the heavy lifting done by Zscaler is done in the network," he tells Dark Reading.

Kurtz said CrowdStrike's next-generation endpoint sensor already has network traffic inspection and proxy capabilities that should help with integration. Asked during the call by Deutsche Bank analyst Brad Zelnick how the deal would affect CrowdStrike's single-software agent architecture, Kurtz reiterated that commitment without providing a delivery date for the combined agent.

Related:Agentic AI Challenges Progress in Confidential Computing

"The brand promise, single agent. That's not going to change," he said.

Dickson believes the combination could change the competitive landscape, identifying Microsoft as the vendor with a comparable breadth while questioning whether it could match the depth of the software giant's combined offerings.

"It fundamentally changes the competitiveness of the industry, 100%," he says.

That does not mean Palo Alto Networks, for example, needs another acquisition to respond. Dickson says it already has the technologies to compete, pointing particularly to its identity capabilities and its CyberArk deal.

Palo Alto Networks is also pursuing a different route into enterprise AI. Its Nov. 18 agreement to acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock would extend its reach into training and deploying open-weight AI models. While CrowdStrike is emphasizing controls over where agents run and communicate, Palo Alto is moving further into the infrastructure used to build and operate enterprise AI.

"They're changing the terms of competition away from functionality to trust," Dickson says of Palo Alto's approach.

Dickson also points to Cisco's expansion in identity, underscoring the wider competition to connect identity with security enforcement.

For other security vendors, Dickson says the Zscaler acquisition increases the importance of partnerships and differentiation by industry or customer size. He says Microsoft’s broad security portfolio already required that approach; the CrowdStrike-Zscaler combination would add another large platform competitor.

"You need as many friends as you can, and then niche as hard as you can,”"Dickson says.

For CISOs, the competitive shift also raises the question whether a broader platform can simplify security operations without limiting product choice.

After closing, CrowdStrike intends to bring Zscaler's offerings into Falcon Flex, allowing customers to expand across both portfolios through the same subscription model. Podbere said cross-selling and broader adoption would help generate approximately $1 billion in annualized revenue savings within 30 months after closing.

Deutsche Bank's Zelnick asked what the transaction would mean for customers that want another endpoint or secure access service edge (SASE) provider. Kurtz emphasized the single-agent strategy rather than detailing how those mixed-vendor deployments would work.

Separately, responding to a question about vendor lock-in, Kurtz said CrowdStrike would continue working with outside technologies and accepting data from other vendors.

Dickson says coexistence with competing network security products is already common, and he does not see the acquisition itself as a reason for those customers to change course. Deeper integration could make adding Zscaler more attractive to existing CrowdStrike customers, he says.

Despite his enthusiasm, Dickson says the CrowdStrike-Zscaler combination needs stronger identity capabilities to deliver on its AI-agent security ambitions. Discovering an agent and inspecting its traffic are not the same as establishing its identity and determining precisely what it is authorized to do.

Agents need a registry, authentication tied to their identities, and fine-grained authorization, Dickson says, though he questions whether either company’s current portfolio fully provides that combination of capabilities.

CrowdStrike is working to address that area. During the investor Q&A, Kurtz said the company expects to introduce an agent identity provider around January, with controls intended to provide just-in-time access and zero standing privileges across human, machine, and agent identities.

Dickson says the challenge is expanding as employees outside software development gain the ability to build agents. Security teams must contend not only with more agents but also with greater autonomy and creators who may lack experience building secure applications.

#9666. Lessons From The Jellyfish Case File

The Green Standard Editing Protocol for Internet Publishing.

The Green Standard Editing Protocol for Internet Publishing.

The Green Standard Editing Protocol for Internet Publishing.

That was Sara Jane Osborn's answer when someone asked who might know what she saw over Anchorage.

She had been taking pictures of a rainbow in June when she spotted something unusual above a distant tree line. It looked like a dark jellyfish, so she started recording. The video lasted about three minutes and eventually went viral in November.

The footage, however, left some important questions unanswered. Nobody could tell how big the object was or exactly how far away it was.

A similar-looking object filmed over Iraq received a much closer examination. The Pentagon's unidentified-object office reviewed 17 minutes of footage, along with the recording details and viewing angles. Its conclusion? With moderate confidence, the object was a cluster of balloons.

The difference between these two cases will allow us to examine how often we make claims in our writing without giving readers enough information to verify them.

The Anchorage object is what happens when there's not enough information to support a conclusion. Writers often run into a similar problem when they half-remember something they read years ago and present it as a fact.

Empty claims often come disguised as convincing statements. Here are some common examples:

"Studies show." Which studies? Who conducted them? How many people were involved? A sentence like "Studies show that waking at 5 a.m. makes people more productive" sounds solid until you ask those three questions.

"Experts agree." Which experts? Are they researchers, practitioners, or people with a large following? If you can't identify them, the statement doesn't carry much weight.

Suspiciously neat statistics. "90 percent of people struggle with this" sounds like a proper statistic. But where did it come from? Who was surveyed? How many people took part? A number doesn't become evidence simply because it has a percentage sign.

The word "best." Best according to whom? Best for what purpose? And compared with which alternatives? Without some context, it's an empty label.

Like the Anchorage video where we couldn’t establish the object’s size, distance, or exact position, writing articles that include claims without backed-up data makes it difficult to investigate.

If a sentence can't answer at least the first three, it is probably a jellyfish.

A reader who spots an unsupported statement may start questioning the entire article. Even the claims you've carefully researched can lose credibility because of one sentence you couldn't verify.

The problem goes beyond individual writers, too. When there's no reliable information to establish what something is, people can attach almost any explanation to it. That's what happened with the Anchorage footage. Claims without evidence leave room for speculation, and speculation can spread quickly.

So, how do you catch these problems before publishing?

Start by reading your draft and highlighting every sentence that states a fact, gives a number, or explains why something happened. Then run each one through the four questions. For every one that fails, choose one of four moves.

Add the evidence. Give the number, the source, or the date.

Shrink the claim. Say only what you saw. "In my case" or "among the 12 people I asked" is honest and strong.

Label it as opinion. "I think" costs nothing and protects your credibility.

Cut it. If the article reads fine without the sentence, then take it out. Not every thought needs to make it to the final draft.

Before you hit publish, go back to the boldest claim in your article and ask yourself how much? Compared with what? Says who? When? If you have the answers, include them. If you don't, make the claim smaller, present it as an opinion, or take it out altogether. Whatever you do, don't leave your readers staring at another mysterious jellyfish.

#9665. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

This entry was posted on Tuesday 13th of October 2026 07:24 PM

One has to wonder how big the backlog of flaws is at this point. Maybe this month’s increase in the number of fixes just reflects an increasing number of people working on these fixes, and that they already have enough flaws to keep them all busy for a long time. Oh to be a fly on the wall.

Why do I still own and use a computer for my business?

For every invention, product, or process that man creates, several other problems are created for him. There never seems to be an end. I am glad that humans are actually testing the vulns that are discovered by LLMs, but for how long will that be the case? How long until the LLMs themselves well be checking there own vuln discoveries, testing and deploying with no human involvement…….

It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then:

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

Note: An old philosopher said that if we ever did produce something like an AI android, we would very shortly be very, very ashamed of ourselves.

I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.

This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing. Again.

So, what’s the patch record for Linux? search says patches published anywhere from 5~10 days after public notices are posted, not easy to match Microsoft’$ record…

Linux is starting to accept LLM vulnerability requests and they’re finding some flaws that have been around for decades. The total number is likely less, at least for the Linux kernel, but full distros use a large number of projects to create their OS and each of those pieces will have their own vulnerabilities.

See for example: https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/status/release/stable

That shows what’s currently being worked on for Debian. The first column notes the specific package the CVE refers to.

Should we call it a vulnerability if no attacker has any interest in it? I’m seeing a flood of vulns getting patched, but I’m not seeing a flood of vulns causing breaches…

If someone can make your mom stop, cry, and fork over a twenty to an animal shelter talking about puppies in a subway station, that is still a vulnerability of your mother, even if she is fortunate enough not to be approached on any one single given day of her daily commute.

I expect better analogies from you from here on in young man.

#9664. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9663. Industrial Serial Gateways Broadcast That They're Insecure

Critical OT access devices will often tell you, and anyone else, whether they're protected by authentication — and many aren't.

Internet scans indicate that some substantial fraction of serial device servers deployed at operational technology (OT) sites worldwide not only lack authentication but broadcast the fact publicly.

We all have a friend or a family member who's deeply insecure, and it's obvious as soon as they start talking. The same can be said of serial-to-IP gateways. Recently Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher for Flare, probed the wider Internet for these sorts of devices, finding that a substantial chunk of them are discoverable. Worse, they often responded to straightforward requests by saying whether they were or were not protected by authentication — and many were not.

An insecure serial-to-IP gateway is a serious risk to anyone downstream of it. These devices are responsible for translating information between the Internet and industrial machinery. So in a cyberattack, a reachable and unauthenticated one can inadvertently translate an Internet-based threat into one that affects major, safety-critical machines.

Related:How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Using a specific vendor's UDP discovery service, rather than probing all vendors' devices, Cheek found 2,474 serial-to-IP gateways exposed on the Web. They seemed to map to real devices rather than honeypots, with half of them located in Russia.

For some reason, in response to the researcher's unsolicited probes, around half of the devices — 1,265 — proffered their authentication status. Of those that did, 973 reported that authentication was disabled. In other words, 39.3% of all Internet-exposed gateways visibly lacked authentication, and among those whose status could be gleaned, that figure was 77%.

"These devices ship with authentication off. An integrator sets one up on a bench, gets the meter or the drive or the Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) talking to the SCADA host, and moves on to the next site," Cheek laments. "The device then does one job for 10 or 15 years, and nobody logs into it again. In many cases, the operator doesn't even know it exists because it went in as part of someone else's equipment."

There are also understandable, if not entirely justifiable reasons why operators fail to conceal and lock down their serial device servers. Cheek cites a multitude of reasons, including that enabling such scurity features can break software on the host side.

"Older SCADA packages and virtual serial port drivers may not support the secured modes, so an operator who switches them on can lose the link to the field," he says. "Then someone has to drive to an unstaffed site to fix it. Firmware updates carry the same risk at a remote site with no spare on hand. People who have been burned by that once are slow to touch a working device again."

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Still, an exposed, unauthenticated serial gateway is a welcome mat for bad actors. Not only does it give arbitrary actors entry into sensitive OT systems and eliminates the need to exploit any kind of vulnerabilities, it also allows attackers to use the vendor's own supplied tools, which could blend malicious activity in with normal IT-OT traffic.

Cheek made special mention of the risk to mobile network operators and, even more specifically, private access point name (APN) service providers. Last year's Polish power grid attack used a private APN to pivot from a wind farm's network to the power plant where the attackers ultimately shut down a steam turbine, water treatment system, and seven serial-to-IP devices. According to Flare, 322 of the 2,474 discovered devices in the study lived in address space associated with known mobile network operators in Europe and the Middle East.

OT operators can begin to secure their OT access layer by first doing an inventory of the devices they're running. "For every cellular unit, find out what plan the SIM is on and whether it gets a public address. Then ask your carrier in writing whether devices on your private network can reach each other or devices belonging to other customers," Cheek notes. "Don't assume the managed product isolates them. In the Polish incident, that missing isolation is what let the attacker move between two unrelated organizations."

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Next, he advises, "Lock down the data ports as well as the login. Most of these devices let you restrict which IP addresses can open a connection. Configure them so only the SCADA host can reach the serial ports and only an engineering workstation can reach the management interface. Switch off the services you don't use, which on most units means the discovery service, Telnet, older SNMP, and often the Web interface. Remove SSH and Telnet entirely from anything that faces the carrier network," and plop a strict firewall between the gateway and control network.

There are also general practices organizations can put in place, like ensuring that the next time they purchase serial device servers, a person or team is assigned to be responsible for the devices, and that they have necessary credentials, configuration, and network details from system integrators.

At the end of the day, though, nothing compares to preventing an attacker's ability to find and speak to a device in the first place.

"Even a fully patched gateway with authentication on is usually connected to equipment on the serial side that has no security of its own," Cheek points out. "A meter, a drive, or an RTU will accept any correctly formed command that reaches it. So the useful question is who can reach the gateway at all, because whoever can reach it gets whatever is behind it. Authentication and patching both matter, but restricting what can reach the gateway does more good than either."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9662. Ginger VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?


Ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market. This article aims to highlight the specifics of each one so that you can make a more informed decision about the one you'll use.

What is Grammarly?

If you are a writer, you must have heard of  Grammarly before. Grammarly has over 10M users across the globe, it's probably the most popular AI writing enhancement tool, without a doubt. That's why there's a high chance that you already know about Grammarly.

But today we are going to do a comparison between Ginger and Grammarly, So let's define Grammarly here. Like Ginger, Grammarly is an AI writing assistant that checks for grammatical errors, spellings, and punctuation. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

While the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

Features of Grammarly

  • Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a personal dictionary 
  • Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Understand inconsistencies. 
  • Detect unclear structure. 
  • Detect Plagiarism.
  • Explore overuse of words and wordiness. 
  • Get to know about the improper tones. 
  • Discover the insensitive language aligns with your intent, audience, style, emotion, and more.


What is Ginger

 Ginger is a writing enhancement tool that not only catches typos and grammatical mistakes but also suggests content improvements. As you type, it picks up on errors then shows you what’s wrong, and suggests a fix. It also provides you with synonyms and definitions of words and allows you to translate your text into dozens of languages.


Ginger Software: Features & Benefits

  • Ginger's software helps you identify and correct common grammatical mistakes, such as consecutive nouns, or contextual spelling correction.
  • The sentence rephrasing feature can help you convey your meaning perfectly.
  • Ginger acts like a personal coach that helps you practice certain exercises based on your mistakes.
  • The dictionary feature helps users understand the meanings of words.

In addition, the program provides a text reader, so you can gauge your writing’s conversational tone.


Ginger vs Grammarly

Grammarly and Ginger are two popular grammar checker software brands that help you to become a better writer. But if you’re undecided about which software to use, consider these differences:

  • Grammarly only supports the English language while Ginger supports 40+ languages.
  • Grammarly offers a wordiness feature while Ginger lacks a Wordiness feature.
  • Grammarly shows an accuracy score while Ginger lacks an accuracy score feature.
  • Grammarly has a plagiarism checker while ginger doesn't have such a feature.
  • Grammarly can recognize an incorrect use of numbers while Ginger can’t recognize an incorrect use of numbers.
  • Grammarly and Ginger both have mobile apps.
  • Ginger and Grammarly offer monthly, quarterly, and annual plans.
  • Grammarly allows you to check uploaded documents. while Ginger doesn't check uploaded documents.
  • Grammarly Offers a tone suggestion feature while Ginger doesn't offer a tone suggestion feature.
  • Ginger helps to translate documents into 40+ languages while Grammarly doesn't have a translation feature.
  • Ginger Offers text to speech features while Grammarly doesn't have such features.


Grammarly Score: 7/10

Ginger:4/10

So Grammarly  wins here.

Ginger VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • Ginger offers a Premium subscription for 13.99$/month. it comes at $11.19/month for quarterly and $7.49/month for an annual subscription with 40$ off.
  • On the other hand,  Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly, and $12/month for an annual subscription.

For companies with three or more employees, the Business plan costs $12.50/month for each member of your team. 

Ginger Wins Here

Ginger vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons


Grammarly Pros

  • Offers  free version
  • All-in-one tool (grammar checker + spell checker + punctuation checker)
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Style checker (paid version)

  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Free mobile apps 
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Can upload and download documents


Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy

Ginger Pros

  • Offers free version
  • All-in-one tool (grammar checker + spell checker + punctuation checker)
  • Affordable Subscription plans (Additionals discounts are available)
  • Active and passive voice changer
  • Translates documents in 40+ languages 
  • Personal dictionary
  • Browser extension available 
  •  Personal trainers help clients develop their knowledge of grammar.
  • Text-to-speech feature reads work out loud
  • Get a full refund within 7 days


Ginger Cons

  • Mobile apps aren't free
  • Limited monthly corrections for free users
  • No style checker
  • No plagiarism checker
  • Not as user-friendly as Grammarly
  • You are unable to upload or download documents; however, you may copy and paste files as needed.
  • Doesn't offer a free trial


Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

While both writing assistants are fantastic in their ways, you need to choose the one you want. 

For example, go for Grammarly if you want a plagiarism tool included. 

Choose Ginger if you want to write in languages other than English. I will to the differences for you in order to make the distinctions clearer.

  • Grammarly offers a plagiarism checking tool
  • Ginger provides text to speech tool
  • Grammarly helps you check uploaded documents
  • Ginger supports over 40 languages
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX
Both Ginger and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. Depending on your needs, you might want to use Ginger over Grammarly. As per my experience, I found Grammarly easier to use than Ginger.

Which one you like let me know in the comments section also give your opinions in the comments section below.

#9661. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

This entry was posted on Wednesday 14th of October 2026 10:22 AM

“Sanctions” can include fines. A fine by itself doesn’t stop the company from continuing to do business whereas being named in full multi-national sanctions prevents UK-aligned businesses/individuals from doing so with them. Although if they’re able to just switch the name and ownership and/or move infrastructure/ops to a new 3rd party host, it’s probably just more whackamole than not.
